chapter: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
title: Mixed bands and the merging of the black and white unions
summary: Willard and Collette discuss segregated bands at the Cotton Club and the post-war push to merge the two unions, with Howard commenting.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: At the Cotton Club, apparently they had some engagements where they were all-white bands and some engagements where they were all black bands.
Just a couple more things and then we can get out of here.
Is that the way it worked?
I don't know.
They weren't all white bands or either all black?
I don't know.
Well, I hadn't really heard of white bands working at the club, but I guess they did.
Well, there was no mixing of colored and white at the time.

Charlie Barnett told me (inaudible) they had jam sessions. He said he remembered jamming with black musicians, friends of his in a church in Watts after lots of places but between the bandstand he said it couldn't be done hours and (inaudible) in L.A.
That's about the way it was, yeah.

Because I'm pretty like not really sure, even when we got into it, we didn't see very much of mixing. Maybe a occasional record date or something, where they needed a soloist who had a certain sound or something, they would get in, but as far as -- do you know about when they began to work together, say, on a steady job, or was that much later, in the

'40s, because naturally after the war, World War II, when, say, I came back, a bunch of us, they were beginning to a little bit but still not very much because the unions were still -- there were still two unions, which meant -- do you remember that, when we came back from the service, -- and then we'll wind up here -- getting the two unions together because there was a period when some white people or either Mexicans, Rene Block, one, wanted to get into the black union and I think he got in but then there was some ruling that he couldn't stay in.
They wouldn't let him stay.
Yeah, things like that had to be cleared up.
And he was working at the union.
Yeah, right.
I know it.
He said he felt like he would belong to 767.
I knew Rene. -- because he was playing.
Like Johnny Otis at the time, I remember Johnny had just about all black band except maybe Rene (inaudible). But at that period there were very few bands that were mixed.
You were around then.
What's that?
You were around then.

Yes, I was around in that period. That's what I'm saying. I wanted to know before that. I guess there was none either, because in that period we began to try to do something about it, and that's how getting the unions to amalgamate was in our minds very strongly at that point, especially after being in the service for a few years and knowing what could happen there.
You know one thing? The only thing about -- they would just take people and try to push them out to work and instead of trying to get them something that would be concrete. You know what I mean?
They would push them out to work?
Yeah, push them out to work, you know.
Into certain jobs that --
Yeah.
What do you mean, that they didn't want to do?
That they didn't want to do and things like that.
Uh-huh. Well, anyway, I think that gives us something to go on for this period. But everything's working out fine.
Okay.
Okay? All right, Paul. So thanks again for all that time.
